fatal_errors: The proposed V-for-Mo substitution does not reconstruct the demonstrated intervention, which was cold rolling of Nb35Zr26Ti19Hf15Mo5 followed by controlled recovery/recrystallization annealing.
None of the cited evidence directly supports V substitution in Nb-Zr-Ti-Hf-Mo, preservation of approximately 1700 MPa compressive yield strength, or a 20–30% plastic-strain increase.

The assertion that lowering electronegativity disparity will make dislocation motion more uniform and improve ductility without weakening the alloy is speculative; replacing Mo with lower-modulus V could instead reduce solid-solution strength.
The notation NbZrTiHfMo_(1-x)V_x is inconsistent with the stated 5–10 at.% total-alloy substitution and leaves the tested compositions ambiguous.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the requested strength–plasticity problem and provides a controlled composition series with measurable falsification criteria, so it is experimentally testable. However, it misses the target alloy, processing route, tensile conditions, and work-hardening/recovery/recrystallization mechanism. The target evidence shows that rolling raises tensile strength while reducing elongation and that annealing progressively restores elongation at a strength cost; the generated quantitative prediction concerns a different compressive alloying strategy. Its boundary of retaining a single BCC phase below roughly 10 at.% V is explicitly stated but not substantiated. The cited papers offer only generic HEA or solid-solution context and unrelated Mo/B2 observations, not prior evidence for the proposed V intervention or its numerical performance prediction. Thus the proposal is a testable compositional idea but is insufficiently supported to qualify as a well-evidenced plausible alternative.
